title: Name days
hookLine: many Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate their saint's day

cards: A phone buzzes before breakfast. Then again, and again. By lunch, a man named Nikos has a stack of messages, a call from his aunt, and a tray of pastries waiting at work.

It isn't his birthday. It's his name day: the feast of Saint Nicholas, the saint he's named for. Tonight, friends may drop by without being invited, because on a name day, in his family, the door is open.
In some Orthodox and Catholic families, a name day is celebrated as warmly as a birthday.

teach.h: A SAINT'S DAY BECOMES YOUR DAY.
teach.b: In Catholic and Orthodox life, saints are remembered on particular days of the year. If you're named for a saint, that saint's day becomes your day too. Some go to church that morning; some families eat together.

The saint is a companion, someone who walked the road before you. Hebrews pictures the faithful who came before as a crowd in the stands: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses."
A name day picks one face out of that cloud and says: this one is yours. Next, a naming in Luke. Elizabeth has a son in her old age, and the neighbors want to call him Zacharias, after his father.
Elizabeth says no, he'll be called John.

Zacharias, who can't speak, asks for a writing tablet: "His name is John. And they marvelled all." In John's Gospel, Jesus gives Simon a new name: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone."
A name, and a calling with it.

teach.h: I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.
teach.b: Then Isaiah: "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Isaiah speaks to Israel, a whole people, and still the phrase is personal.

teach.h: A WHITE STONE, A NEW NAME.
teach.b: Last, Revelation, the Bible's last book: the one who overcomes is given "a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it."
Not every church keeps name days; others honor the saints in other ways. But the thread holds: in this faith, a name has a story.

how: Some Orthodox and Catholic Christians celebrate the feast day of the saint they are named for, often with church in the morning, a family meal and visits from friends; in Orthodox tradition a child is often given a saint's name at baptism.

games.q: you're Zacharias. you can't speak, and everyone wants your newborn son named after you. what do you do?
o: nod, and let them name him Zacharias.
ask for a tablet and write: his name is John.
leave the choice to the neighbors.
games.why: he writes "His name is John." "and they marvelled all." the name came with a story before the boy could speak.

practice: Think about your own name: who gave it to you, and why, and whether a saint shares it, or part of it. Some names have no saint, and they still have a story.
If you pray, you can hear Isaiah's words, I have called thee by thy name, as spoken to you; if you don't, just sit with the name you've carried all your life.

wordCard.voice: Name days. The feast of the saint you're named for, kept by some Catholic and Orthodox Christians as a day of their own.
